questions.prompt: Given `struct point { int x, y; } a = {1, 2}, b;` what does `b = a;` do?
options: Makes b an alias of a
Copies every member of a into b
Does not compile: structs cannot be assigned
questions.explain: Structs are values in C: assignment copies all members. `b` is an independent copy; changing `b.x` afterwards does not affect `a`.
option_notes: C has no aliases; that would need a pointer.

questions.prompt: To access member `x` through a pointer `p` to a struct, write `p{{0}}x`.

questions.explain: A struct groups members; they are initialised in order and accessed with a dot.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Assignment copies.)
questions.explain: `b = a` copies all the members: `b` is an independent copy, so changing `b.x` does not touch `a`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (. and ->.)
questions.explain: With a pointer to a struct `q->x` is the same as `(*q).x`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (The function gets a copy.)
questions.explain: A struct passed by value is copied: `reset` clears its own copy. Pass a pointer (`struct p *`) to modify the caller's struct.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (On x86-64 Linux; padding.)
questions.explain: The int must be aligned to 4 bytes, so the compiler inserts 3 padding bytes after the char: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. `sizeof` of a struct can be larger than the sum of its members.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (typedef and an array of structs.)
questions.explain: `typedef` gives the struct a short name. `a[1].id` is 2 and 1.5 + 2.5 is 4.0.

questions.prompt: Can you compare two structs with `a == b`?
questions.explain: The `==` operator does not work on structs. Compare each member (and strings with `strcmp`). A byte-wise `memcmp` can be wrong because of padding.
options: No: compare them member by member
Yes, it compares all the members
Yes, but only if they have no pointers
option_notes: It does not compile at all.

questions.prompt: What does `typedef struct node { int v; struct node *next; } Node;` define?
questions.explain: `typedef` creates an alias for a type: after it you can write `Node n;` instead of `struct node n;`. (Inside the struct you still need `struct node *` for `next`.)
option_notes: typedef declares a type name, not a variable.
Node is the struct itself, not a pointer.

questions.prompt: Why is the member `next` in `struct node { int v; struct node *next; };` a POINTER and not a `struct node`?
questions.explain: Every node would have to contain another whole node, forever. A pointer has a fixed size, so lists and trees are built with pointers.
options: A struct cannot contain itself: it would have infinite size
The compiler requires the name next
Structs may not have more than one member
option_notes: Size, not speed, is the reason.

questions.prompt: `(*p).x` can be written more simply as {{0}}.
questions.explain: The arrow `->` combines the dereference and the member access.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of inserting a new node at the front of a linked list in order.
questions.explain: Link the new node to the old list BEFORE changing the head, otherwise the old list would be lost.
items: Allocate the new node with malloc
Store the value in the new node
Make the new node's next point to the current head
Make the head point to the new node
